transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?

Lately I can’t think straight at work—decisions that used to be easy now leave me stuck and second‑guessing everything. It actually got to the point where my HR partner noticed my decline in concentration and referred me here for an evaluation.
Have these concentration problems been happening after a specific stressful or upsetting event, and if so, how long have they been going on?

Yes, it really spiraled after I was promoted to lead a high-visibility lean transformation project, which came with intense performance pressure and constant travel. This current low spell and the fog in my head have been dragging on for about three months now.
Since this started, have you also been feeling persistently sad or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, or has it been more mainly anxiety and stress about the work situation?

It’s definitely more than just work stress. For the past few weeks, it has felt like this heavy, gray film has settled over everything, leaving me feeling utterly hollow and on the verge of tears for no clear reason.
Did your symptoms start within a month of the work promotion and pressure, or did they begin later and keep going even after the stress eased?

Looking back, I’ve actually noticed milder cycles of these highs and crashes since my mid-twenties. But this current severe low spell started about three months ago, right around the most intense phase of the project rollout, and it has been dragging on continuously ever since.
Have you had periods of feeling unusually energized, needing much less sleep, more talkative, or more confident than usual in the past?

Yes, just a couple of weeks before this crash, I had a phase where I was buzzing with excitement, sleeping only three or four hours a night without feeling tired. My coworkers even joked I was on "1.5x speed" because I was talking so fast and taking on endless extra projects. I also felt this intense confidence, honestly believing that I alone could turn our whole division around.
Have you ever had a period lasting at least several days when you felt unusually high, energetic, or irritable with much less need for sleep, and it caused problems at work or in your relationships?

Yes, absolutely—just a couple of weeks before this crash, I was buzzing with excitement, sleeping only three to four hours a night, and talking so fast my coworkers joked I was on "1.5x speed" while I packed my calendar. I also got incredibly irritable and would snap at people over tiny delays. I've had these cycles since my mid-twenties, but this recent one was so intense it became impossible for my coworkers to ignore.

Have you ever had a period like that lasting at least 4 days, or 1 week if it was severe, where you felt unusually energized or irritable with much less sleep and it clearly caused problems at work, with money, or in relationships?

Yes, those high-energy phases typically last for weeks at a time, and I've experienced them since my mid-twenties. During those times, I'd sleep only three to four hours a night, talk at "1.5x speed," and over-commit to projects because I felt completely fine. While I used to think it was just a highly productive cycle, this last episode caused major issues at work and triggered this severe crash where my manager had to address my plummeting performance.

During your high-energy periods, have you ever had hallucinations or believed things that other people said were clearly not true, such as feeling specially chosen, having unusual powers, or being watched?

No, I've never had hallucinations, felt watched, or thought I had supernatural powers. But I did have a very inflated sense of confidence, genuinely believing that I was the only one who truly understood the project and that I could single-handedly turn our entire division around.

opening_question.question: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview confirms a recurrent bipolar course with distinct past episodes of elevated/irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, pressured/rapid speech, increased goal-directed activity/overcommitment, inflated self-confidence, and clear work impairment, followed by a current depressive episode with low mood, tearfulness, and impaired concentration. There is no psychosis. This is most consistent with bipolar affective disorder (F31).
